tagline.text: A memorial park on the site of the old Pangatian POW camp

location.label: Location
location.text: Pangatian, Cabanatuan City, Nueva Ecija, along the Nueva Ecija–Aurora Road

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 hours (a full day as a round trip from Manila)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱700~2,500 (same-day trip from Manila, bus round trip plus local transport; free admission)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Clark International Airport (CRK) or Manila Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL)

children.text: This is a World War II prisoner-of-war memorial park in Pangatian, northeast of Cabanatuan city proper. Survivors built the memorial on the old camp grounds in 1982, and the site also has a marker about the rescue of January 30, 1945 and a Filipino memorial.
The Cabanatuan American Memorial stands about
7km

northeast of Cabanatuan city proper in Nueva Ecija, in the village of Pangatian along the Nueva Ecija–Aurora Road. The American Battle Monuments Commission (ABMC), the U.S. agency that cares for the site, describes it as about 4.5 miles northeast of the city and about 85 miles north of Manila. Wikipedia places it on the Cabanatuan–Palayan road in Barangay Pangatian, about
8km

north of the city proper, so the sources describe the direction a little differently but point to the same place. It is not a resort stop. Go knowing it is a quiet place of remembrance where you stay a while and read history.

The grounds were once Camp Pangatian, a military training camp used for about 20 years before the war. After the Japanese occupation began it became an internment camp for Allied prisoners, and prisoners from Camp O'Donnell and elsewhere are said to have been moved here around mid-1942. Wikipedia says more than 20,000 American and Allied servicemen and civilians were held at the camp. The memorial wall is said to carry the names of 2,656 Americans who died here.

The memorial was dedicated on April 12, 1982 by survivors of the Bataan Death March and the Cabanatuan camp. The ABMC has run and maintained it since 1989. Besides the ABMC-managed area, the grounds include a Philippine historical marker recording the raid of January 30, 1945 and a second memorial for Filipino guerrillas opened by the Nueva Ecija provincial government in 2003, so one visit lets you see both the American and the Filipino perspectives.

The visit itself is short. One review says the new memorial area alone takes about 30 minutes. For that reason many travelers combine it with Cabanatuan city sights or other war sites such as the Capas National Shrine and make a full day of it. This guide assumes a same-day trip from Manila, and items that change often, such as hours, entrances and renovation work, are marked as things to confirm on site.

The ABMC's official guidance asks visitors to treat the site as hallowed ground, like a burial ground. Wikipedia describes the names and ranks of the servicemen held at the camp inscribed in horizontal rows, similar to the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, with a marble altar at the center. Lower your voice in front of the wall of names and read them slowly.

On the night of January 30, 1945, the U.S. Army's 6th Ranger Battalion, the Alamo Scouts and Filipino guerrillas raided the camp and freed some 500 prisoners. According to Wikipedia the figure varies slightly between accounts, and one tally gives 522 rescued, made up of 489 prisoners and 33 civilians. The Philippine historical marker records that guerrillas under Captains Juan Pajota and Eduardo Joson held off Japanese reinforcements.

On April 6, 2003 the Nueva Ecija provincial government opened a second memorial area next to the ABMC site. It honors the Filipino guerrillas who helped in the rescue and is said to include two National Historical Institute (NHI) tablets, one in Filipino and one in English. Do not leave after reading only the American side; the notes here give the story its balance.

blocks.title: The Soldier's Trust marker and the West Point memorial

children.text: A U.S. war memorials database lists three memorials on the grounds: the rescue marker, "The Soldier's Trust" marker honoring the defenders of Bataan and Corregidor, and the West Point Philippines Defense Memorial. Read each inscription in person instead of relying on photos alone.

blocks.title: The American and Philippine flags side by side

children.text: Wikipedia says this is the only place in Nueva Ecija where the American flag flies beside the Philippine flag. It also describes a rooftop mural of Filipino and American soldiers helping each other. Whether the mural and facilities are unchanged may differ because of renovation work, so check for yourself.

Wikipedia records that on April 6, 1982 President Ronald Reagan signed a joint resolution designating April 12 as a memorial day for the Cabanatuan prisoners of war. Events may be held around this date each year, but I could not confirm whether or when. On event days there is less time to visit quietly, so keep that in mind.

blocks.title: Read ahead through film and books

children.text: The rescue was depicted in the 2005 film The Great Raid, and the book Ghost Soldiers tells the same story. The film dramatizes parts of the story and may differ from fact, so compare it with the explanations at the memorial before or after your visit.
Board a Cabanatuan-bound bus at the Five Star terminal in Cubao. Departures are said to run hourly from
to
, but confirm locally.
Arrive at the Cabanatuan terminal, buy water and snacks, and arrange a ride to Pangatian and a way back.
Arrive at the memorial and first take your time with the wall of names and the altar in the ABMC area.
Read the Philippine historical marker and the guerrilla memorial area, and compare them with what you know from the film or books.
Return to the city for lunch. For sights in town, see the Cabanatuan History and Civic Spaces entry.
If time allows, walk around St. Nicholas of Tolentine Cathedral and Plaza Lucero.
Check the last bus to Manila and head back early.
The memorial itself takes little time, so travel takes up most of the day. If leaving from Manila feels like too much, you could stay a night in Cabanatuan or Clark.
Start at the Capas National Shrine in Tarlac, the end point of the Bataan Death March.
Travel by vehicle toward Nueva Ecija. The time can vary greatly with road conditions.
At Pangatian, continue the story of what followed in the prison camps.
Go into the city to eat and arrange transport back.
The two sites cover different camp stories, so packing both into a single day can be emotionally heavy. Leave plenty of time.
Direct buses to Cabanatuan run from the Five Star terminal in Cubao, Quezon City. The Pamasahe site lists a regular seat at
via SCTEX with a travel time of about
4 hours
, and the route via Bulacan at
Pamasahe says departures from Cubao run hourly from
to
and from Cabanatuan every 30 minutes from
to
. Fares may rise with fuel surcharges and schedules change without notice, so confirm with the company before you travel.
From the Cabanatuan terminal you continue to Pangatian by jeepney, tricycle or similar. I could not confirm routes or fares, so ask locally.
Travel time differs by source, from about 2.5 to 4 hours. Allow plenty of time for traffic.
The distance from Manila to Pangatian is roughly
140km
, though it varies greatly with road conditions. This figure is converted from the ABMC's roughly 85 miles.
Some operators run Manila day tours that combine Capas and Pangatian. Prices and itineraries vary by operator, so ask them directly.
The memorial is in Pangatian along the Nueva Ecija–Aurora Road, and searching Google Maps for "Cabanatuan American Memorial" brings up the location. Some visitors say the entrance was hard to find.
If you do not arrange a return ride, you may be stuck around dusk. If you negotiate a wait or a round trip, agree on the fare first.
It is an outdoor memorial park, so weather matters a lot. You will walk in places with little shade, so earlier hours are more comfortable.
The ABMC lists official hours as daily
to
, though Trip.com, Waze and others differ slightly. Hours may change on holidays or during renovations, so confirm before you go.

items.label: Admission
items.note: ABMC official guidance: no reservation needed

items.label: Local transport, Cabanatuan to Pangatian
items.note: Jeepney, tricycle or hired vehicle, by negotiation

items.label: Lunch
items.note: Based on city restaurants; there may be no restaurant near the memorial

items.label: Day tour
items.note: Some tours combine Capas and Pangatian

There seem to be no suitable hotels or restaurants near the memorial, so it is safer to handle meals and lodging in Cabanatuan city. The city has local food such as longganisa and large hotels, so an overnight stay works. For city information, see the Cabanatuan History and Civic Spaces entry.
Buy water and snacks in the city beforehand and carry out your trash. Eating loudly or drinking alcohol inside a memorial park is discourteous.

Watching the film The Great Raid or reading the book Ghost Soldiers beforehand makes the explanations on site much easier to follow. Some parts are dramatized, so give priority to the records at the site.
Visit both the ABMC area and the Filipino memorial area. They carry different perspectives.
Save the exact location on an offline map in Google Maps. Some reviews say the entrance was hard to find.
Leaving early in the morning helps you avoid the heat and leaves more room for return transport.
Check the ABMC website's visit-planning page again before departure for hours and renovation status.
Carry small cash. Cash is easiest for jeepneys and tricycles.
Seeing the Capas National Shrine as well helps you connect the story from the Bataan Death March to the prison camps.

This is a place of remembrance. Do not climb on the wall of names or monuments or pose for playful photos. One review from January 2026 says the main gate was under renovation and visitors entered by a rear gate, so check the current access.
The ABMC asks visitors to respect the site as hallowed ground. Avoid loud voices, drinking and smoking.
Reviews say parts of the older memorial area are weathered and damaged, and the new memorial area is inside a fence. The current condition may differ.
I could not confirm whether drones or commercial filming are permitted, so follow the instructions on site.
It is a different place from the Manila American Cemetery. Enter the place name precisely when using maps.
Do not stay around dusk without arranging return transport.

A walking route through the old center, including St. Nicholas of Tolentine Cathedral, Plaza Lucero and Freedom Park. The ABMC puts the memorial about 4.5 miles from the city; confirm travel time locally.
A memorial near the end point of the Bataan Death March, where you can continue the story of the same war. It is in Tarlac, so it needs a separate trip.
A river gorge park in Nueva Ecija, a choice if you want a nature break after the war sites. Confirm distance and travel time locally.
